chapter_note.about: Relational algebra is a small language for asking questions of tables. Every operator takes tables and returns a table, so you can nest them like arithmetic. This chapter starts from what a relation is, then covers selection and projection, set operations, products and joins, outer joins and division, which is the "for all" query. It then covers rewriting a query so the selection runs early, tuple relational calculus and safety, and the key and foreign-key facts that bound result sizes. GATE questions mostly give small tables and ask you to run one expression, so the habit is to compute each sub-expression as a set and then combine.
chapter_note.simple: Think of a spreadsheet. Selection picks the rows you want, and projection picks the columns you want, keeping a repeated line only once. A join glues two sheets together wherever a shared column agrees, and an outer join also keeps the lines that found no partner, with blanks for the missing side. Division finds the people who did every item on a list. One rule runs through all of it: a table is a set, so repeated lines do not exist. Tuple calculus says the same things in logic words, and exam questions give small tables to work through by hand.

cards.title: Relational model basics
cards.simple: A relation is just a neat table with a name, like a class register. The columns have fixed names, such as roll number, name and marks. The number of columns is the degree. Each row is one record, called a tuple, and the number of rows is the cardinality. There is one rule that surprises people: a relation is a set, so the same row cannot appear twice, and the order of rows does not matter. Shuffling the register gives the same register. In exam words: a relation is a set of tuples over named attributes; degree is the number of attributes, cardinality is the number of tuples.
cards.idea: A **relation** is a named table: a set of **tuples** (rows) over a fixed list of **attributes** (columns). The **degree** is the number of attributes. The **cardinality** is the number of tuples. Because a relation is a *set*, it has no duplicate tuples and no row order.
cards.definition:
A relation $R(A_1,\dots,A_k)$ is a finite subset of $\text{dom}(A_1)\times\cdots\times\text{dom}(A_k)$.

- **Degree** of $R$ = $k$ = number of attributes.
- **Cardinality** of $R$ = $|R|$ = number of tuples.
- Maximum cardinality = product of the domain sizes. A key on one attribute lowers it to that attribute's domain size.
- Three schema levels: external (views), conceptual (tables), internal (storage).
cards.intuition_full: Why call it a set? Because the model came from mathematics: a relation between domains is a collection of tuples, and a collection of distinct things has no repeats and no order. This is why projection must remove duplicates and why the union of two relations has no repeated rows. It also explains an upper bound GATE likes: a relation over domains of sizes 3, 2 and 4 can hold at most 3 × 2 × 4 = 24 different tuples, because there are only that many possible tuples to choose from. A key makes the bound tighter: if the first attribute is a key, two tuples can never share a value in it, so you can have at most as many tuples as that attribute has values. Keep two words apart: attributes are the columns (degree), tuples are the rows (cardinality). People swap them under pressure.

So at most 3 tuples.

(1,a) appears twice and (2,b) appears twice.
The distinct tuples are (1,a), (2,b), (3,c).
examples.answer: 3 tuples. A list of rows is not a relation until duplicates are removed. (SQL tables are bags and would keep all 5.)

cards.title: Selection and projection
cards.simple: Think of a class register. Selection is like asking "show me only the students who scored above 50": you keep whole rows, but fewer of them. Projection is like asking "just give me the list of departments": you keep only one column, but all the rows. Here is the catch: if three students are from CS, the list would say CS three times, but a relation is a set, so CS appears once. So selection shrinks the number of rows, and projection can shrink rows too, because duplicates collapse. In exam words: σ_cond(R) keeps the rows that satisfy the condition and all columns; π_A,B(R) keeps the listed columns and removes duplicate rows.
cards.idea: **Selection** $\sigma_{cond}(R)$ keeps the rows that satisfy a condition and keeps all columns. **Projection** $\pi_{A,B}(R)$ keeps only the listed columns, and because the result is a set, **duplicate rows are removed**. Projecting dept from six employees in three departments gives three rows, not six. You can nest them: evaluate the innermost operator first.
cards.definition:
- $\sigma_{c}(R)=\{t\in R\mid c(t)\}$. Same schema as $R$; $|\sigma_c(R)|\le|R|$.
- $\pi_{X}(R)$ = the sub-tuples on attributes $X$, as a set. Schema is $X$; $|\pi_X(R)|\le|R|$.
- Conditions use $=,\ne,<,>,\le,\ge$ and $\wedge,\vee,\neg$.
- Cascade: $\sigma_{c_1\wedge c_2}(R)=\sigma_{c_1}(\sigma_{c_2}(R))$.
- A projection removes columns, so a later selection cannot use a dropped column.
cards.intuition_full: Selection works on rows and projection works on columns, and that is the whole difference. Selection never changes the shape of a row, so it can only reduce the count. Projection changes the shape, and since the narrower rows may now coincide, the set rule merges them. This is why the count after a projection can be smaller than the count before it, and why the order of operators matters: selecting first, then projecting, uses the full row for the test. Projecting first and then selecting fails if the condition mentions a column that has been thrown away. When you evaluate a nested expression, read it from the inside out: the innermost operator runs first, and its output is a fresh relation with its own schema. Write down that intermediate relation, with its rows, before you apply the next operator.

cards.title: Set operations
cards.simple: Take two class lists, R and S, that have the same columns. Union is everyone on either list, with names that appear on both listed once. Intersection is the people on both lists. Difference R minus S is the people on list R who are not on list S. Difference is different from the others: R minus S and S minus R are not the same. You can only compare two lists if they have the same kinds of columns in the same order, like comparing two class registers with identical columns. In exam words: union, intersection and difference need union-compatible relations (same number of attributes with matching domains). The results are sets.
cards.idea: Union $R\cup S$, intersection $R\cap S$ and difference $R-S$ treat relations as sets of tuples. They work only on **union-compatible** relations: the same number of attributes, with matching domains in the same positions. Difference is not symmetric: $R-S$ and $S-R$ differ. All three return sets, so duplicates never appear.
cards.definition:
For union-compatible $R$ and $S$:

- $R\cup S$: tuples in $R$ or $S$ (or both).
- $R\cap S$: tuples in both. Also $R\cap S=R-(R-S)$.
- $R-S$: tuples in $R$ but not in $S$.
- $|R\cup S|=|R|+|S|-|R\cap S|$.
- The result takes the attribute names of the first operand.
cards.intuition_full: These are the ordinary set operations, with one extra requirement: a tuple from R has to be comparable to a tuple from S, so both must have the same shape. The inclusion-exclusion formula |R ∪ S| = |R| + |S| − |R ∩ S| is the quickest way to count: add the sizes, then subtract the double-counted shared tuples. For bounds, a union is smallest when one relation is inside the other (size = max) and largest when they share nothing (size = sum). An intersection is smallest when they share nothing (0) and largest when one contains the other (size = min). A difference R − S is smallest when S contains as much of R as possible. Intersection is a derived operator, because R ∩ S = R − (R − S).

examples.setup: R(id, x) = {(1,a), (2,b), (3,c)} and S(id, x) = {(2,b), (3,c), (4,d)}. Compute R ∪ S, R ∩ S, R − S and S − R.
steps: Both relations have two attributes, so they are union-compatible.
Union: all tuples of R, plus those of S not already in R: (1,a), (2,b), (3,c), (4,d). 4 tuples (3 + 3 − 2 shared).
Intersection: (2,b) and (3,c). 2 tuples.
R − S: tuples of R missing from S: (1,a).
S − R: tuples of S missing from R: (4,d).

Intersection is smallest when they share nothing: 0. Largest when S ⊆ R: 4.
R − S = |R| − |R ∩ S|. Largest when the intersection is 0: 6. Smallest when the intersection is 4: 2.

cards.title: Product and joins
cards.simple: Imagine two lists. One lists departments, the other lists employees with their department number. If you pair every department with every employee, you get a huge pile of pairs, most of them nonsense. That pile is the cross product. A join keeps only the sensible pairs, the ones where the department number is the same on both sides. A natural join does this automatically for every column the two lists share, and shows each shared column only once. A department with no employees, and an employee with an unknown department, find no partner, so they disappear. In exam words: R × S has |R|·|S| tuples; a theta join is a product followed by a selection; a natural join equates all common attributes and keeps one copy of each.
cards.idea: The **Cartesian product** $R\times S$ pairs every tuple of R with every tuple of S: $|R|\cdot|S|$ tuples and all columns. A **theta join** $R\bowtie_\theta S$ is a product followed by a selection with condition $\theta$. A **natural join** equates all attributes with the same name and keeps one copy of each. Tuples with no match vanish from the result.
cards.definition:
- $R\times S$: schema = attributes of R then S; $|R\times S|=|R|\cdot|S|$.
- $R\bowtie_\theta S=\sigma_\theta(R\times S)$.
- $R\bowtie S$ (natural): equality on every common attribute, one copy of each in the result.
- If R and S have **no** common attribute, $R\bowtie S=R\times S$.

cards.intuition_full: Think of the join in two stages, even though a database engine never builds the full product. Stage one: imagine every possible pairing, which is the product. Stage two: throw away the pairs that do not satisfy the condition. This view makes counting easy. The number of rows after the join is the number of pairs that agree on the join columns, so for each value v of the join attribute, multiply how many R rows have v by how many S rows have v, and add over all v. That product per value is why a join can be bigger than either input (many-to-many) and why it can also be smaller (unmatched rows vanish). In the natural join, the shared column appears once in the schema because the two copies are always equal. Two special cases are worth remembering: no common attribute gives the full product, and all attributes common gives the intersection.

cards.title: Outer joins
cards.simple: An ordinary join is picky: if a team has no players, that team does not show up in the result. Sometimes you want to see everyone, even those without a partner. An outer join does that: it keeps the lonely rows and fills in the missing part with blanks (NULL). A left outer join keeps every row from the left list, a right outer join keeps every row from the right list, and a full outer join keeps both. The ordinary matches are always there; the outer join just adds the lonely rows on top. In exam words: left, right and full outer joins add the unmatched tuples of the kept side(s), padded with NULL, to the inner join.
cards.idea: A **left outer join** $R ⟕ S$ keeps every tuple of R. Where R has no match in S, the S columns are padded with NULL. A **right outer join** keeps every tuple of S. A **full outer join** keeps both. The matched rows are exactly the inner join. So: *outer join = inner join + unmatched rows with NULL padding*.
cards.definition:
Let $J=R\bowtie S$ and $U_R$ = tuples of R with no match in S, $U_S$ = tuples of S with no match in R.

- Left outer: $J\ \cup\ (U_R\times\{\text{NULL}\})$.
- Right outer: $J\ \cup\ (\{\text{NULL}\}\times U_S)$.
- Full outer: $J\ \cup\ (U_R\times\{\text{NULL}\})\ \cup\ (\{\text{NULL}\}\times U_S)$.
- $|R ⟕ S| = |J|+|U_R|$ and $|{\rm full}| = |J|+|U_R|+|U_S|$.
cards.intuition_full: The best way to count outer joins is to treat them as three groups that do not overlap: the matched pairs (the inner join), the unmatched tuples of the left relation, and the unmatched tuples of the right relation. A left outer join is the first two groups, a right outer is the first and third, and a full outer is all three. That makes the containment obvious: the full outer join contains the left and right outer joins, and each of them contains the inner join. NULLs in the padded columns are not values, so a later test such as C = 7 on a padded row is unknown, not false, and the row is dropped by a selection. That is why a selection on the padded side after an outer join turns it back into an inner join, and why pushing such a selection below the join changes the answer (r7).

cards.title: Division and double difference
cards.simple: Some questions say "find everyone who did all of these", for example which supplier supplies every part on the list. One way to find them: for each person, check the whole list, and if even one item is missing, they are out. That is division. Another way: build all possible (person, item) pairs, remove the real pairs, and what is left are the missing pairs. Anyone who appears in a missing pair is out, and everyone else is in. The key rule: the list must be the complete reference list, not a list built from the data you are testing. In exam words: R(A,B) ÷ S(B) returns the A values paired in R with every B value in S, equal to π_A(R) − π_A((π_A(R) × S) − R).
cards.idea: **Division** $R(A,B)\div S(B)$ returns the values of A that are paired in R with **every** B value in S. It answers "for all" questions. Equivalent form (**double difference**): take all A values, and remove those for which some pair $(a,b)$ with $b\in S$ is missing from R. The divisor S must be the full reference set.
cards.definition:
$R\div S=\pi_A(R)-\pi_A\bigl((\pi_A(R)\times S)-R\bigr)$

- $\pi_A(R)\times S$: every pair (candidate a, required b).
- Subtract $R$: the **missing** pairs.
- $\pi_A$ of those: candidates with something missing.
- Subtract from all candidates: those with nothing missing.
- Schema of the result: attributes of R not in S. Extra B values in R that are not in S are ignored.
cards.intuition_full: The double difference is just the same sentence in algebra: "keep a, unless there exists a required b such that (a,b) is not in R". The two subtractions say "all candidates minus the bad ones". Reading it as a double negative also explains why it expresses "for all": for all b in S, (a,b) is in R is the same as not (exists b in S with (a,b) not in R). If S is empty, there is no required b, so nobody can be bad, and every candidate qualifies. The most common error is building the divisor from the dividend: dividing by π_p(Supplies) means "supplies every part that somebody supplies", which is easier than "supplies every part in the catalogue". Unsupplied catalogue parts then slip past. Always take the divisor from the relation that lists the complete set (the catalogue, the required courses).

cards.title: Equivalences and pushdown
cards.simple: Suppose a list of 1,000 orders must be matched with 10 shops, and then you keep only shop "Delhi". You could match everything and then throw most results away. Or you could first pick the one Delhi shop, and then match only that. Both give the same answer, but the second does far less work. This trick is called pushing the selection down: filter early, before the expensive join. It is safe in a normal join. It is not safe on the side that gets blanks in an outer join, because the blanks are made after the match. In exam words: a selection on attributes of one relation can move below the join onto that relation. Do not push a selection into the NULL-padded side of an outer join.
cards.idea: Two expressions are **equivalent** when they return the same relation on every database. A selection that uses only one relation's attributes can move **below a join** onto that relation, so the join sees fewer tuples. A conjunction splits: $\sigma_{a\wedge b}=\sigma_a\sigma_b$. This pushdown is safe for **inner** joins, but not into the padded side of an **outer** join.
cards.definition:
- **Cascade of selections:** $\sigma_{c_1\wedge c_2}(R)=\sigma_{c_1}(\sigma_{c_2}(R))$.
- **Selection and join:** if $c$ uses only attributes of $R$, then $\sigma_c(R\bowtie S)=\sigma_c(R)\bowtie S$.
- **Selection over a conjunction with both sides:** $\sigma_{c_R\wedge c_S}(R\bowtie S)=\sigma_{c_R}(R)\bowtie\sigma_{c_S}(S)$.
- Joins are commutative and associative; projections can be pushed too, keeping the join attributes.
- **Outer join:** $\sigma_c(R⟕S)\ne R⟕\sigma_c(S)$ when $c$ uses S.
cards.intuition_full: Why is pushdown valid for an inner join? A joined tuple exists only when its R part and its S part both exist and match. A condition on the R part only filters R parts. Filtering R before or after pairing gives the same set of surviving pairs. The gain is the size of the intermediate result: a smaller R means fewer pairs to consider. Optimisers do this automatically. Why not for outer joins? An outer join manufactures rows that have no S part, padded with NULL. A condition on S then says "false/unknown" for those manufactured rows, so selecting after the join discards them. If you filter S first and then outer-join, the unmatched R rows are still manufactured with NULL and kept. The two orders disagree. This is the classic exam trap, and the cure is a two-row counterexample.

cards.title: Tuple relational calculus
cards.simple: Algebra tells you how to compute the answer step by step, like a recipe. Calculus describes what the answer looks like, like a wish. For example: "give me every t such that there is an employee u with the same name and a salary above 50". You are not told how to find it; you describe it. The letter t is the answer slot, and the letter u is a helper that checks every row of the table. Wherever the sentence says "there is some u", that matches projection, and where it adds conditions, that matches selection. In exam words: TRC writes {t | P(t)} with free tuple variable t; ∃ (exists) variables become joins or projections; ∀ (for all) becomes a double negation or division.
cards.idea: **Tuple relational calculus** writes a query as $\{t\mid P(t)\}$: the set of tuples $t$ for which the formula $P$ is true. The variable $t$ is **free** (it names the answer). Other variables are **bound** by $\exists$ (there is a tuple) or $\forall$ (for all tuples). Existential variables correspond to projection and join; $\forall$ is expressed with a double negation, like division.
cards.definition:
- $\{t\mid t\in R\wedge\ c(t)\}$ = $\sigma_c(R)$.
- $\{t\mid\exists u\in R\,(t[A]=u[A]\wedge c(u))\}$ = $\pi_A(\sigma_c(R))$.
- $\{t\mid\exists u\in R\,\exists v\in S\,(t[A]=u[A]\wedge u[B]=v[B]\wedge c(v))\}$ = $\pi_A(R\bowtie\sigma_c(S))$.
- $\forall x\,P \equiv \neg\exists x\,\neg P$.
- Exactly one free variable: the answer tuple.
cards.intuition_full: Read a TRC query as a test. Imagine going through every candidate tuple t and asking the formula. For an expression with ∃u, you try every row of the table u ranges over and see if any one passes. When the test uses u[A] to define t[A], t is just a copy of that part of u, which is exactly a projection of u. When the test also links u to another variable v through equality, that is a join. A ∀ is the same idea with "every row passes". Since ∀x P = ¬∃x ¬P, the same double negation appears in the algebra for division. The free variable t is the only one that is not bound by a quantifier; counting free variables is a classic multiple-choice question. Translating in either direction needs three steps: find the answer attributes (projection), find the conditions (selection) and find the links between variables (join).

cards.title: Safety and expressive power
cards.simple: Imagine asking a librarian: "Give me every book that is NOT on the shelf." The answer is every book in the world, an endless list, so the question cannot be answered. That kind of question is unsafe. A safe question always stays inside the data you have: "books on the shelf that are not red". Relational algebra can only ask safe questions. It is also limited in other ways. It cannot add up numbers or count, and it cannot follow a chain of unknown length, like "everyone who is an ancestor of Ravi" through parent, grandparent and so on. In exam words: basic relational algebra is exactly as expressive as safe tuple calculus; it has no aggregates and no recursion (transitive closure).
cards.idea: A calculus expression is **safe** if it always returns a finite relation. A negation alone is unsafe: $\{t\mid\neg(t\in R)\}$ returns every tuple *not* in R, which is infinite. Safe expressions keep $t$ tied to a relation. **Relational algebra is exactly as expressive as safe calculus.** Basic algebra cannot do **aggregates** (count, sum) or **transitive closure** (recursion).
cards.definition:
- **Safe:** every answer tuple has all its values drawn from the relations or constants in the query, so the answer is finite.
- Unsafe examples: $\{t\mid\neg(t\in R)\}$, $\{t\mid t[A]>5\}$, $\{t\mid t\in R\vee t[A]=1\}$ (a disjunct not tied to a relation).
- Safe examples: $\{t\mid t\in R\wedge\neg(t\in S)\}$, $\{t\mid\exists u\in R(t[A]=u[A])\}$.
- **Codd's theorem:** algebra $\equiv$ safe TRC.
- Outside basic algebra: aggregates, grouping, and recursion such as transitive closure.
cards.intuition_full: Safety is about the size of the answer. An expression that says "everything except R" has to scan an infinite universe, so it can never finish. Algebra avoids the problem by construction: every operator takes finite relations and returns a finite relation. Calculus is looser, so we require that the formula bounds t to a relation. Expressive power is a second, separate question: which finite answers can be written at all? Codd's theorem says safe calculus and algebra can express the same set of queries. But some natural queries are in neither. Counting needs an aggregate operator that the pure model does not have. Transitive closure (all ancestors, all reachable cities) needs a join repeated an unknown number of times. A fixed expression has a fixed number of joins and finds paths up to a fixed length. SQL adds aggregates and, in newer versions, recursive queries, which is why SQL is more powerful than the basic algebra.

cards.title: Keys, FK and size estimates
cards.simple: Say each student has one unique roll number, and a marks sheet has many lines per student. If you pair students with their marks lines, each marks line finds exactly one student, or none, so the number of pairs can never be more than the number of marks lines. It is not "students times lines": the unique roll number puts the cap on the count. A foreign key is a promise that every roll number on the marks sheet really exists in the student list. In algebra the promise reads "marks roll numbers minus student roll numbers is empty". For guessing how many rows a condition keeps, multiply the chances, if the two tests are independent. In exam words: a key on the join attribute of S gives |R ⋈ S| ≤ |R|; a foreign key from r1.B to r2.C means π_B(r1) − π_C(r2) = ∅.
cards.idea: If the join attribute is a **key** of S, each R tuple matches **at most one** S tuple, so $|R\bowtie S|\le|R|$. A **foreign key** from $r_1.B$ to $r_2.C$ is the promise that $\pi_B(r_1)-\pi_C(r_2)=\emptyset$ (every child value exists in the parent). With a foreign key (and no NULLs) the join has exactly $|r_1|$ tuples. For estimates, an OR of independent conditions has selectivity $s_1+s_2-s_1s_2$.
cards.definition:
- **Key side bound:** if $B$ is a key of $S$, then $|R\bowtie_B S|\le|R|$.
- **Foreign key as an assertion:** $r_1.B\to r_2.C$ holds iff $\pi_B(r_1)-\pi_C(r_2)=\emptyset$. The subtraction goes child minus parent.
- With a foreign key (and B not NULL): $|r_1\bowtie r_2|=|r_1|$.
- **Selectivity** of a condition = fraction of tuples that satisfy it. Independent AND: $s_1s_2$. Independent OR: $s_1+s_2-s_1s_2$. Disjoint conditions on one attribute: $s_1+s_2$.
cards.intuition_full: A key means "at most one row per value". For a join on that value, every R row finds zero or one partner, never two, so the join cannot be bigger than R. Without the key the bound would be the product |R| · |S| in the worst case. The foreign key goes one step further: it removes the zero. Each child value is guaranteed to exist among the parent values, so every R row has exactly one partner. The assertion checks "is there a child value that is not a parent value?", and that is a difference of two projections. The direction is child minus parent: wrong direction would ask whether the parent has values nobody uses, which is allowed. For selectivity, use probability: if A and B are independent, the chance that a row passes A-or-B is one minus the chance it fails both, 1 − (1 − s1)(1 − s2) = s1 + s2 − s1 s2. If both tests look at the same attribute with disjoint ranges, a row cannot satisfy both, so there is nothing to subtract and the chances just add.

examples.setup: Same r(A, B), 2000 tuples, A uniform on 1..25. Estimate σ_(A≤5)∨(A≥21)(r). Does the independent-OR formula still work?
steps: Selectivity of A ≤ 5: 5/25 = 0.2. Selectivity of A ≥ 21: 5/25 = 0.2.
Both conditions are about the same attribute. No value is both ≤ 5 and ≥ 21: the conditions are disjoint.
So the selectivities add: 0.2 + 0.2 = 0.4. Estimate 2000 × 0.4 = 800.
The independent formula would give 0.4 − 0.04 = 0.36, so 720. That wrongly subtracts an overlap that does not exist.
examples.answer: 800 tuples. For disjoint conditions on the same attribute, add the selectivities. The independent-OR formula is for independent attributes.

scenes.title: A relation is a set of tuples over named attributes

steps.caption: A relation is a named table: Movie(mid, title, year, genre, rating). Each row is a tuple.
Columns are the attributes. This relation has 5 of them, so its degree is 5.
Rows are the tuples. There are 4 of them, so its cardinality is 4.
Try to insert the tuple (m2, Raja, 1999, comedy, 7) again. A relation is a set, so a duplicate tuple adds nothing.

set.text: the duplicate is not a new tuple

steps.caption: Row order does not matter either. The same four tuples listed in reverse order are the same relation.

scenes.title: Selection filters rows, projection keeps columns

steps.caption: Emp has 6 tuples. We evaluate π_dept(σ_sal>50(Emp)) from the inside out.
Selection σ_sal>50 keeps the rows whose sal is above 50: Asha 60, Chen 75, Dev 55, Esha 80. Bala (45) and Farid (40) are dropped. All columns are kept.
Projection π_dept keeps only the dept column of those 4 rows. That gives CS, CS, ME, EE.

set.text: keep column dept: CS CS ME EE

steps.caption: A relation is a set, so the two CS rows merge into one. The result has 3 rows, not 4.

scenes.title: Union, intersection and difference of two relations

steps.caption: R and S both have the same attributes (id, x), so they are union-compatible. Each has 3 tuples.
Union R ∪ S: every tuple that is in R or in S. The shared tuples (2,b) and (3,c) appear once. 4 tuples.
Intersection R ∩ S: only the tuples in both: (2,b) and (3,c). 2 tuples.
Difference R − S: tuples in R that are not in S. Only (1,a). 1 tuple.
Difference is not symmetric. S − R is {(4,d)}, a different result. Order of the operands matters.

scenes.title: Cross product pairs everything, a join keeps the matches

steps.caption: Dept has 3 tuples and Emp has 4. They share the attribute did.
Cross product Dept × Emp pairs every Dept row with every Emp row: 3 × 4 = 12 pairs, with all 4 columns.
A natural join keeps only the pairs where did is equal. Dept 1 matches e1 and e2. Dept 2 matches e3. The other 9 pairs are dropped.
Dept 3 (EE) matches no employee, and e4 has did 4 which is in no Dept. Rows with no match disappear from an inner join.
The join result keeps one copy of did: columns (did, dname, eid), 3 rows.

scenes.title: Outer joins keep unmatched rows and pad with NULL

steps.caption: Team and Player share tid. The lines show the pairs where tid matches: Red with p1 and p2, Blue with p3.
Inner join: only the matching pairs. 3 rows. Team 3 (Green) and player p4 (tid 9) are lost.
Left outer join: keep every Team row. Green has no player, so its pid is padded with NULL. 4 rows.
Right outer join: keep every Player row. p4 has no team, so tname is NULL. 4 rows.
Full outer join keeps both unmatched rows: 3 matches + Green + p4 = 5 rows. It contains the inner, left and right results.

scenes.title: Division: who has every part in the divisor?

steps.caption: Supplies(s, p) lists which supplier supplies which part (✓). The divisor Parts = {p1, p2, p3}. Find the suppliers that supply every part of the divisor.
s1 supplies p1, p2 and p3: all three. Keep s1.

set.text: s1: has p1 p2 p3 → keep

steps.caption: s2 has p1 and p3 but p2 is missing. Reject s2.
s3 has p1, p2, p3 and also p4. Extra parts outside the divisor do not matter. Keep s3.

set.text: s3: has all of p1 p2 p3 → keep

steps.caption: s4 supplies only p2: p1 and p3 are missing. Reject s4.
The same answer by double difference: all (supplier, part) pairs minus the real ones leaves the missing pairs (s2,p2), (s4,p1), (s4,p3). Remove those suppliers from all suppliers.

set.text: suppliers with a missing pair: s2, s4

steps.caption: Result: {s1, s3}.

scenes.title: Push the selection below the join

steps.caption: Query: employees of the CS department, σ_dname='CS'(Emp ⋈ Dept). Emp has 6 rows (e1..e6) and Dept has 3 (CS, EE, ME). Two plans give the same answer.
Plan A: join all of Emp with all of Dept first. The join produces 6 rows, then σ keeps the 2 in CS. Work: a 6-row intermediate result.
Plan B: apply σ to Dept first. Only 1 Dept row is left (CS). Then join Emp with that one row.

set.text: Plan B: σ leaves 1 Dept row

steps.caption: The join in Plan B produces only 2 rows. The final answer is the same 2 rows, but the join handled far less data.
Pushdown rule: a condition on one relation's attribute can move below the join onto that relation. The result is equivalent and cheaper.

scenes.title: Evaluating a tuple calculus query row by row

steps.caption: The free variable t ranges over answer tuples. The bound variable u ranges over Emp. t is in the answer if some u exists with the same name and sal above 50.
u = row 1 (Asha, sal 60): 60 > 50 is true. So Asha joins the answer.
u = row 2 (Bala, sal 45): 45 > 50 is false. This row gives nothing.
u = row 3 (Chen, sal 75): 75 > 50 is true. So Chen joins the answer.
u = row 4 (Dev, sal 50): 50 > 50 is false. This row gives nothing.
u = row 5 (Esha, sal 80): 80 > 50 is true. So Esha joins the answer.
The answer has 3 tuples: Asha, Chen, Esha. The ∃u becomes a projection, and the condition becomes a selection.

scenes.title: Safe versus unsafe calculus, and what algebra cannot do

steps.caption: A relation R is a finite set of tuples. The space of all tuples of the same shape is infinite.

set.text: finite R inside an infinite universe

steps.caption: { t | ¬(t ∈ R) } asks for every tuple that is NOT in R: the whole universe except R. That is infinitely many tuples, so the query is unsafe.
{ t | t ∈ R ∧ ¬(t ∈ S) } also uses negation, but t must come from R. The answer stays inside the finite set R. It is safe, and equals R − S.

set.text: safe: stays inside R  (= R − S)

steps.caption: Algebra equals safe calculus. Both cannot express recursion: from parent edges a→b→c→d, the ancestor relation (dashed edges) needs a loop of unknown depth. Counting and summing also need extensions.
The dashed arrows are the transitive closure: a→c, b→d, a→d. A fixed number of joins finds only paths of fixed length.

scenes.title: A key on one side bounds the join size

objects.colTitle: S(B, C)  B is a key

steps.caption: R has 7 tuples. S has 4 tuples and B is its key, so each B value appears at most once in S.

set.text: |R| = 7,  B is a key of S

steps.caption: Each R row can match at most one S row, because the B it carries appears at most once in S. Look at the lines: every R row has one line or none.

set.text: each R row: at most 1 match

steps.caption: R row (a7, 4) has no line: S has no B = 4. So the join has 6 rows, which is at most |R| = 7.
Foreign key test: B in R should reference B in S. The assertion is π_B(R) − π_B(S) = ∅. Here the difference is {4}, not empty, so there is no foreign key.
If the foreign key held, every R row would find its partner: |R ⋈ S| would equal |R| exactly. A key bounds the join size by the other side, never by the product 7 × 4 = 28.
